summary: Defines a DHCP sub-option for the CableLabs Client Configuration option. It tells cable devices to invalidate security tickets that they have stored in non-volatile memory. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: A cable box may keep a saved security pass. This memo adds a message telling it to throw the pass away.

questions: what is the dhcp ccc security ticket control sub-option
what is a ticket control mask
how does a cable device invalidate stored security tickets
subtitle: A DHCP sub-option that lets a cable provider tell a device to throw away its saved security tickets.

tldr.problem: Cable devices may keep Kerberos-style security tickets in non-volatile memory so they can skip slow ticket acquisition after a power cycle. Service providers still need a way to force those tickets to be dropped, for example for testing or diagnostics.
tldr.mechanism: A new sub-option (code 9) in the DHCP CableLabs Client Configuration option carries a 16-bit Ticket Control Mask. Each bit stands for one server or server group, and a 1 tells the device to invalidate its stored ticket for it immediately.
tldr.outcome: Providers can force re-establishment of security associations on demand. The RFC notes that a malicious DHCP server could abuse this to disrupt a deployment, but argues the cable network design makes that unlikely.

today: RFC 3594 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by any later RFC.

sections.title: Why Tickets Need Remote Control
sections.content:
The CableLabs Client Configuration (CCC) option, defined in RFC 3495, carries several sub-options used to configure devices in CableLabs architectures. Those architectures use the PacketCable Security Specification, which is based on Kerberos V5 (RFC 1510), so that devices can authenticate and set up security associations with application servers.

Devices are allowed to keep security tickets in local persistent storage. A power-cycled device can then avoid the expensive step of acquiring a ticket again, as long as the stored ticket has not expired. The RFC says this greatly reduces the security overhead of a deployment.

The catch is that the service provider loses control over how long those tickets live. The provider needs that control for operational functions such as forcing re-establishment of security associations, remote testing and remote diagnostics. This sub-option supplies it.
sections.eli5: Saving a pass saves time, but the cable company sometimes needs everyone to get a new one. This memo gives it a way to ask.

sections.title: The Players and Acronyms
sections.content:
The RFC defines a handful of acronyms. CCC is the CableLabs Client Configuration option. A CCD (CableLabs Client Device) is any device that uses it, and a PacketCable MTA is one example. An MTA (Media Terminal Adapter) is the CCD specific to the PacketCable architecture. STC is Security Ticket Control, the CCC sub-option this document defines.

PacketCable itself is described as a multimedia architecture developed by CableLabs. The RFC points to external CableLabs documents for the full details and notes that the PacketCable Security Specification is based on Kerberos V5 but is not a strict implementation of it.
sections.eli5: A CCD is the gadget in your home, like a phone adapter. STC is just the name of the new message that tells it about its saved passes.

sections.title: The Sub-Option Format
sections.content:
The sub-option is four bytes: a Code of 9, a Len of 2, and a two-byte Ticket Control Mask (TCM) written as m1 and m2. The length MUST be 2. The TCM is an unsigned 16-bit quantity in network byte order.

Each bit of the mask is assigned to a specific server or server group. The mask tells the device which application server tickets to validate or invalidate.
sections.eli5: The message is a tiny checklist of switches. Each switch is for one server, and it can be on or off.

sections.title: What the Bits Mean
sections.content:
A bit value of 0 means the device MUST apply the normal invalidation rules, defined in the PacketCable Security Specification, to the locally stored ticket for that server or group. A bit value of 1 means the device MUST immediately invalidate the stored ticket for it.

Bit 0 is the least significant bit. Bit 0 is the PacketCable Provisioning Server used by the device. Bit 1 is the group of all PacketCable Call Management Servers used by the device. Bits 2 through 15 are reserved and MUST be set to 0.

Two rules keep things safe for older or simpler devices. A device that does not locally store tickets MUST ignore the sub-option. Bit values the device does not know MUST be ignored.
sections.eli5: A zero means keep going as usual. A one means tear up that pass now. If your gadget does not keep passes, or does not know a switch, it just ignores it.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA assigned a sub-option code from the CableLabs Client Configuration sub-option number space, which lives in the BOOTP-DHCP Parameters Registry. IANA also set up a new registry there, called the CableLabs Client Configuration Option Ticket Control Mask Bit Definitions. Its initial entries are the bits described in the previous sections.

Future bit definitions are registered under an IETF Consensus approval policy, as described in RFC 2434.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of what each switch means. New switches can only be added if the community agrees.

sections.title: Abuse by a Rogue DHCP Server
sections.content:
The RFC points to existing discussion of DHCP attack exposure in RFC 2131 and RFC 3118, plus additional CCC exposure in RFC 3495.

The new sub-option could itself be used to disrupt a deployment. If a large number of MTAs are reset or power cycled, start their provisioning flow, and a malicious DHCP server tells them to invalidate all tickets, they would all try to authenticate and obtain tickets at once. That could cause a Denial of Service condition.

The RFC calls this scenario unlikely. In the required cable architecture the DHCP client reaches the network through a cable modem and the CMTS (head-end router). The CMTS is explicitly configured with the valid DHCP server addresses and, if correctly configured, only allows downstream DHCP traffic from them. This does not stop spoofed DHCP servers behind the CMTS, but that part of the network is assumed to be closely controlled by the service provider.
sections.eli5: If a bad guy could send this message to lots of boxes at once, they would all ask for new passes together and jam the system. The cable network is built so that bad guys have a hard time getting in that spot.

fields.name: Len
fields.desc: Length of the data; MUST be 2.

fields.name: TCM (m1, m2)
fields.desc: Ticket Control Mask, unsigned 16 bits in network byte order.

items.label: Provisioning Server
items.desc: The PacketCable Provisioning Server used by the CCD.

items.label: Call Management Servers
items.desc: The group of all PacketCable Call Management Servers used by the CCD.
